Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
I can't rely on other people
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: John, a 32-year-old park ranger living in North America, has been struggling with severe psychological distress following an intense period of torture he experienced several months ago. The trauma left him deeply scarred and profoundly altered his sense of safety and trust. John’s symptoms are multifaceted, forming complex interconnections that have significantly impacted his daily life. John’s belief that his body is permanently damaged by the torture has made it extremely difficult for him to rely on himself or others, which in turn fuels a pervasive fear that he might be going crazy. This fear leads him to avoid situations where he might feel vulnerable again. For example, John now rehearses conversations meticulously before any social interaction, often feeling numb and detached from his emotions. He avoids driving altogether, fearing the unpredictable nature of being on the road. The memory of the torture remains fragmented for John; some moments are crystal clear, while others are entirely blank. When he attempts to recount these experiences, he finds himself losing track of what he is saying, unable to articulate a coherent narrative. This inability to put his memories into words compounds his sense of vulnerability and reinforces his belief that something irreparably wrong has happened to him. John’s heightened threat perception has been exacerbated by the lingering trauma. He feels an almost visceral reaction to delays or unexpected events, immediately assuming the worst. His body reacts before he can consciously process what is happening, often leading to a surge of panic. For instance, when he was recently assigned to patrol an area with poor cell reception, his heart raced and his mind jumped to catastrophic scenarios, even though rationally he knew there was no immediate danger. John’s fear that something bad will happen has led him to develop obsessive checking behaviors—constantly verifying whether the doors and windows in his cabin are locked. This behavior provides a fleeting sense of control but only temporarily soothes his anxiety. As John continues to avoid driving and rehearse conversations, he finds it increasingly difficult to fulfill his duties as a park ranger. His interactions with colleagues have become strained due to his meticulous planning and avoidance behaviors. The cumulative effect of these maladaptive strategies has further exacerbated his memory problems. John’s constant preoccupation with safety and control leaves him mentally exhausted, making it even harder for him to piece together the fragmented memories from the torture. This cycle creates a self-perpetuating loop where his fear and avoidance behaviors reinforce each other, deepening his conviction that he cannot rely on anyone or anything. What finally brought John to seek help was a significant incident at work where he nearly caused an accident due to his heightened anxiety while driving. He realized that his fear of going crazy and the physical manifestations of his trauma were no longer sustainable. Despite his reservations about opening up, John is hoping for relief from the overwhelming sense of vulnerability and the constant threat he feels lurking around every corner. John’s current state is marked by a deep-seated fear that his psychological distress will only worsen if left untreated. He is most hopeful for a return to some semblance of normalcy in his daily life, particularly in his role as a park ranger where he feels grounded and connected to nature.
